items.title: Louie Bellson — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: I remember when Buddy Rich one time on the Tonight Show – Eddie Shaughnessy was playing drums. Eddie’s a big guy – he sat in on Eddie’s drums.

ctx.x: But you went down to the 20. I guess that was to facilitate having two up there.

Yeah. I was thinking that the tubular – long tube would give me the sound I was looking for. Yet I could put those tom-toms on top of that 20-inch bass drum and not make everything too high, because I always wanted my cymbals to be in a position so I can play rhythm, because today some drummers have – I don’t know how they do that. They play with the cymbals very high, but they still get a sound. To me, I go with Jo Jones, who said, “I like that ride cymbal right there, staring me in the face.” And I like the…
Speaking of size and drummers, we didn’t mention Chick Webb.

items.title: Louie Bellson interviewed by Monk Rowe, Sarasota, Florida, April 12, 1996
items.q: Well Eddie Shaughnessy came to me once and he said “hey, did you really start the two bass drums?

ctx.x: How did, I meant to ask this earlier on, but how did the double bass drum set come to fruition? © Hamilton College Jazz Archive -12-

Well Eddie Shaughnessy came to me once and he said “hey, did you really start the two bass drums? I thought you did, but did Ray McKinley do it first?” I said well I don’t know because when I was a youngster in 1938 I drew the plans for the double bass drum kit. And around 1940, I saw in Down Beat where Ray McKinley was teamed with Will Bradley. They had a band together. They did a lot of boogie woogie things. And there was a picture of him with just two bass drums, see? And so when I saw Ray after that I said…
It must have helped to be a tap dancer I would think.
